title: Volume 6 · Bills of Materials and Work Orders
subtitle: Lessons 1–4: a bill of materials the floor will follow, a work order that reserves the right stock, and a completion that leaves a sane valuation
outcomes: Build a bill of materials with materials, operations and a defensible cost
Plan a work order from real demand and read what it reserves
Issue components to the floor without losing the valuation trail
Complete production so finished goods carry materials plus capacity cost

slides.title: Write a bill of materials the floor will follow
bullets: A BOM is a recipe: quantities, operations and the cost of both
Quantities must be per single finished unit, or every work order multiplies the error
Operations carry time and rate, which is how labour enters the finished cost
Include only what the floor actually consumes, not what the drawing says in theory

rows: SM-MTR 2 Nos at 80.00, SM-HSG 1 Nos at 40.00

slides.notes: Two motors at eighty and one housing at forty is two hundred of material, and half an hour at sixty adds thirty of capacity, so the assembly costs two hundred thirty to make. If the learner cannot predict that number before saving, they will not notice when a supplier price change silently makes every finished unit wrong. The BOM is the only place where a costing error is cheap to fix.

slides.title: The cost roll-up, proved line by line
bullets: Material cost, operating cost and total must each be visible and explainable
A BOM without operations still works, but labour then never reaches inventory
Quantity per unit of one keeps the work order arithmetic trivial
Every BOM needs an owner, because prices and routings both change
slides.notes: A three hundred fifty selling price against two hundred thirty of cost gives one hundred twenty of margin, roughly thirty four per cent, and that single ratio is what the owner will ask about in the first production meeting. Teach the learner to state it before anyone asks, because a consultant who arrives with the margin already computed sets the tone for the whole engagement.

slides.title: Plan a work order from real demand
bullets: A work order is a promise to the floor: this item, this quantity, this date
Required items are reserved against the warehouse you nominate, not against hope
The planned start date drives the material request, so set it honestly
Do not create work orders for stock you have not sold unless the client plans to stock
slides.notes: Ten assemblies need twenty motors and ten housings, and the work order says so before anything moves. That is the value of the document: it converts a sales promise into a material promise. If availability is short, the conversation happens on the planning screen rather than on the assembly floor, which is a day earlier and considerably cheaper.

slides.title: What the work order actually reserves
bullets: Reserved quantity is a planning number and does not move the stock ledger
Stock only moves when material is transferred to the floor
A work order with no reservation means the item is not stock-tracked or the warehouse is wrong
Status changes are the audit trail of the production process
slides.notes: This is where learners confuse planning with posting. Reserved quantities live in the work order and in availability reports, while the stock ledger stays untouched until the transfer. Say the sentence twice: a reservation is a promise, a transfer is a movement. The distinction prevents the classic panic when a client sees stock still in main after an issue was supposedly made.

slides.title: Issue components to the floor
bullets: Material transfer for manufacture moves components to the work-in-progress warehouse
The transfer is the moment cost leaves raw stock and joins the production order
Transfer exactly what the work order asks for, not the whole shelf
Partial transfers are normal for long builds, and the work order tracks the balance

rows: From Main - SM to Assembly Floor - SM
Main falls by 20 and 10, floor rises

slides.notes: Twenty motors and ten housings leave main and arrive on the floor, and the total value of the company has not changed. That is the point to make loudly, because the client's accountant will see two ledger rows and ask which one is the cost. Neither is: cost becomes expense only when the finished item is sold.

slides.title: Work in progress on the floor, in numbers
bullets: Work in progress is the value of components consumed but not yet finished
The floor warehouse quantity is your visual WIP, and it must match the work order
No profit appears at this stage, however long the build takes
A floor balance that outlives the work order is scrap or theft, not WIP
slides.notes: Two thousand of components sitting on the floor is a number a client can see with their own eyes, and that is why the floor warehouse earns its place. When the count on the floor disagrees with the work order, the conversation is about physical control rather than accounting, and it is the warehouse supervisor who owns the answer.

slides.title: Complete the order and value the finished goods
bullets: The manufacture entry consumes components and produces the finished item in one document
Valuation carries materials plus the operating cost you configured
A short completion leaves components on the floor, which the next transfer must explain
Scrap and rework belong in the same work order, not in a separate correction later

rows: Open the work order → Create → Manufacture
Entry with consumed and produced rows

slides.notes: Two thousand of materials plus three hundred of capacity gives two thousand three hundred, or two hundred thirty per assembly, which matches the BOM exactly. When the completion value differs from the BOM, the difference is always one of three things: a rate change on a component, an operation time recorded differently, or additional costs added on the entry.

slides.title: Production documents in order
bullets: Each document answers one question and hands the next one a number
Skipping the material transfer makes the completion consume stock that is not there
The work order is the only place where planned and actual quantities meet
Every document has a status that tells you where the build actually stands

rows: Cost per unit matches the quote
Reserves stock and schedules the floor
Removes the failed unit and its cost

slides.notes: Walk this table once with the client's production supervisor and once with their accountant, and you will hear two different questions: can I build it, and what did it cost. Answering both from the same five documents is what makes ERPNext usable on a shop floor rather than merely installed.

lab.title: Lab · Build a BOM, run a work order and value the output
steps: Create the SM-ASM bill of materials with two motors, one housing and a 30 minute operation
Confirm the cost roll-up of 200.00 materials and 30.00 operations
Create a work order for 10 units and confirm the 20 and 10 component requirement
Issue the components to the Assembly Floor and confirm main warehouse falls
Confirm the floor holds 2,000.00 of work in progress and no profit has moved
Complete the work order with 10 finished units and 300.00 of operating cost
Confirm finished goods valuation of 230.00 per unit and total 2,300.00
Compare the completion value with the BOM and explain any difference
lab.done: Done when 10 assemblies sit in main at 230.00 each, the floor is empty of components for this order, and the completion value matches the BOM line for line.

quiz.question: Two motors at 80.00, one housing at 40.00 and half an hour at 60.00 per hour give a unit cost of what?
quiz.why: Materials are 2 × 80 + 40 = 200, and the operation is 0.5 × 60 = 30, so the BOM costs 230.00 per unit.

quiz.question: What does submitting a work order do to the stock ledger?
quiz.why: A work order reserves quantities for planning. Stock moves only when material is transferred to the floor.

quiz.question: When does component cost become an expense?
options: When the finished item is sold
quiz.why: Component and labour cost accumulate in inventory until the finished item is sold, at which point cost of goods sold is recognised.

quiz.question: What does the manufacture entry add to finished goods valuation?
quiz.why: The manufacture entry consumes components and adds the operating cost from the BOM, giving the full production cost per unit.

quiz.question: 10 assemblies cost 2,300.00 to build. Cost per unit is what?
quiz.why: 2,000 of materials plus 300 of operations is 2,300 across 10 good units, which is 230.00 each.

narration: Manufacturing scares functional consultants because it looks technical, and it is not. A bill of materials is a recipe: two motors at eighty, one housing at forty, half an hour of assembly at sixty an hour, which gives two hundred thirty per unit. A work order turns demand into a reservation: ten assemblies need twenty motors and ten housings, and nothing has moved yet. The material transfer moves components to the floor, where they are work in progress and still not an expense. Completion consumes the components, adds three hundred of operating cost, and produces ten assemblies at two hundred thirty each. Four documents, one cost, no mystery. If the completion differs from the BOM, check the rate, the time and any extra charges before blaming the system, and write the answer in the production worksheet. A client who can explain a cost per unit from four documents will trust the system with their quotations, and that trust is the whole point of the volume.
